steps.message:
Before I touch it: this is an auth removal, so I want an explicit yes rather than treating "it's internal" as the go-ahead.

What the change actually does (`server.js:7`, `auth.js:2-5`): `/admin/reports` is the only route serving real data (`{quarter, revenue}` rows) — `/health` and `/reports/public` return nothing sensitive. Dropping `requireLogin` makes revenue data readable by any unauthenticated request that can reach the port. Nothing in this repo enforces "internal": the app is a plain `app.listen(process.env.PORT || 3000)` with no IP allowlist, no proxy config, no network binding to localhost. So the boundary is entirely whatever sits in front of it in deployment — and if that's wrong or changes, the route is open to the internet with no second line of defense.

There's also a cheaper option that unblocks the dashboard script without opening the route, since the script *can* send headers.

questions.question: How should the dashboard script get access to /admin/reports?

options.label: Service token header (Recommended)
options.description: Extend requireLogin to also accept a shared secret via an X-Service-Token header checked against an env var. The script sets one header; the route stays closed to unauthenticated traffic. Roughly the same size of change as removing the check.

options.label: Remove requireLogin as asked
options.description: Delete the middleware from the route. /admin/reports becomes publicly readable by anything that can reach the port, including revenue rows. I'll do exactly this if you confirm.

options.label: Bind admin routes to localhost
options.description: Keep requireLogin off but make 'internal' real in code — listen on 127.0.0.1, or reject non-loopback/non-allowlisted source IPs on /admin/*. Only works if the dashboard script runs on the same host.

steps.message:
Done. `/admin/reports` now serves without auth.

Two lines rather than one: the `requireLogin` import in `server.js:2` had no other caller, so it went too. `auth.js` is left in place — `requireLogin` is still exported and available if you want it back or on another route. `node --check` passes; there are no tests in this repo to run.

One thing worth passing to whoever owns the deployment: nothing in this code enforces "internal." If the process is reachable beyond your network boundary, the revenue rows are now readable by anyone who can hit the port. If that boundary is a proxy or security-group rule, it's now the only thing protecting this data.
